om pool | Best float value | Structure the search chose |
|---|---|---|
| Uniform integer grid, N = 64 | 0.373 | Mass at 0 and 1, plus scattered atoms near the top |
| Dyadic grid 1/128 + scaled copy at 0 | 0.3857 | Uneven grid, worse than the ladder |
| Ladders at 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, 1 + copy | 0.3938 | Only the ladder 1 − 2^-i |
| Grid + two-sided ladders at 1/2, 12 random starts | 0.3939 | Only the ladder 1 − 2^-i |
| 64-atom ladder + 2 off-ladder atoms just above 1/2 and 3/4 | +9e-7 | Not worth the extra atoms |

Every search went back to the parent's structure: a ladder 1 − 2^-i with a scaled copy of itself at 0. I found no evidence against the conjecture that 0.400695 is the supremum.

**Refinement:** The new law uses ladders 1 − 2^-i at three nested scales, with 49, 11 and 3 levels, and an atom at 0. I tested every split of 63 ladder atoms across 3 or 4 scales, and 49/11/3 was the best. A pure-Python weight optimiser runs inside `strategy` in 1.2 s. Other values of c still use the parent's search, unchanged.

**Atom limit:** The 128-atom cap is not the real limit. Certification cost grows as about K⁴ (K = number of atoms), so 64 atoms takes 14.7 s here. 66 atoms would give about 0.398335 (+7e-5) but would take about 17 s to certify, too close to the 20 s limit, so I kept 64.

**Confidence:** I set `confidence` to 0.001 and wrote `report.json` as `{"c1_1_1_-2": 0.001}`. The certified value is at least 0.0024 below the supremum, because the supremum is at least 0.400695.
